title: Language and Aftermath
premise: For eleven years, Rosalind Delacroix has mailed postcards to her mother's burned-out house in Vercheres Bay, writing the words she never said aloud—apologies, accusations, small daily news—while living invisibly as a professional letter-writer for other people's unsaid things. When the house is put up for auction, Rosalind must return to confront not only the fire that killed her mother and the town that convicted her brother on thin evidence, but her own testimony, given at fifteen, that may have sealed him. As she uncovers what really started the fire and negotiates with the auction, the town, and the brother who refuses her letters even in person, she must decide whether justice belongs to courts or to confession. The novel ends not with exoneration but with Rosalind buying the ruined lot, building nothing on it, and finally mailing her brother a letter addressed to where he actually lives.
about_author: Quentin Sterling is the pen name of a former court stenographer who spent two decades transcribing other people's confessions before turning to fiction. Sterling writes from a coastal town in Atlantic Canada, where the fog is said to keep secrets better than any witness.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. We meet her in her basement flat, cataloguing postcards she's mailed for eleven years to a dead address, and drafting a stranger's apology letter for pay. The beat is quiet complicity: she has built a life out of words that never arrive.

chapters.title: Return to Sender
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. A returned postcard arrives stamped 'addressee unknown'—the post office has finally purged the burned house from its records. That night she learns from a legal notice that 14 Marsh Lane goes to auction in six weeks. The beat is destabilization: her ritual has an expiration date.

chapters.title: The Profession of Other People's Regrets
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. We see her trade in full: love letters to estranged sons, a confession to a dying man's church. A client, Mrs. Okonkwo, asks her to write to a daughter who died, and Rosalind refuses—then can't sleep. The beat is the mirror: she sees what her own unsent letters really are.

chapters.title: Vercheres Bay, Eleven Years Later
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She takes the bus home, unrecognized, and walks past the auctioned lot: charred foundation, weeds, a developer's survey stakes. A neighbor, Gus Thibodeau, half-recognizes her and says her mother's name. The beat is dread wearing the mask of nostalgia.

chapters.title: What the Fire Report Didn't Say
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, with a flashback to age fifteen. At the county records office she reads the official fire report—cause undetermined—and remembers the investigator's questions and her own careful, coached answers. The beat is guilt resurfacing with its original vocabulary intact.

chapters.title: The Brother Who Answers No Letters
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, Rosalind and Emile. Emile Delacroix, out of prison eight years, works a boatyard in the next county and keeps every one of Rosalind's postcards in a tackle box, unopened since the first. His POV reveals he knows something about the fire he has never told anyone. The beat is parallel isolation.

chapters.title: The Auction
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. At the auction she bids against a developer, Alden Voss, who wants the waterfront lot; she wins with money she doesn't have, borrowing against her letter-writing business. The town whispers. The beat is reckless self-exposure—visibility chosen at last, at a price.

chapters.title: Gus Thibodeau's Version
chapters.summary: Gus's POV. The old neighbor, dying of emphysema, tells Rosalind what he saw the night of the fire: a second figure leaving the yard, and Emile's truck gone from the dock an hour before the flames. The beat is the first hard evidence that the truth has more than one shape.

chapters.title: Letters to the Living
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Broke and committed to the lot, Rosalind takes a risky commission: writing letters for Voss, the developer, to soften the town. Working for the antagonist, she learns his own buried grievance against her family. The beat is moral compromise with a paycheck.

chapters.title: The Tackle Box
chapters.summary: Emile's POV. Emile, tracked down by a journalist revisiting the case, nearly burns the postcards, then reads the first one. He drives toward Vercheres Bay, turns back twice. The beat is the pull of the unsaid, stronger than resentment.

chapters.title: Mother's Kitchen, Reconstructed
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Alone on the lot at dusk, Rosalind maps the house from memory—where the stove stood, where the kerosene was kept—and realizes her testimony placed her mother in a room the fire pattern contradicts. The beat is the architecture of memory beginning to crack.

chapters.title: The Witness Who Moved Away
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, road trip. She finds Dana Pell, the prosecution's key teenage witness, now a nurse two provinces away. Dana admits the police fed her details and that she never actually saw Emile that night. The beat is the machinery of the conviction exposed—but Dana won't recant on paper.

chapters.title: Voss Makes an Offer
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Voss offers to buy the lot at triple her cost—and to quietly fund an appeal—if she sells and leaves. Rosalind realizes he wants the land more than he wants the truth, and that his generosity is a leash. The beat is temptation with a hook in it.

chapters.title: Emile at the Gate
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Emile appears on the lot at dawn. Their first meeting in eleven years is all inventory: what each assumed the other knew. He tells her to stop writing to a dead house; she asks him, finally, where he was that night. He walks away without answering. The beat is the wound reopened properly this time.

chapters.title: What Rosalind Saw
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, full flashback. The novel's buried center: fifteen-year-old Rosalind, awake that night, saw her mother strike the match herself—insurance, desperation, the last months of a collapsing life—and said nothing, then said the wrong things when questioned, letting Emile take the suspicion. The beat is devastating self-knowledge.

chapters.title: The Confession Drafts
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She writes and burns seven drafts of a confession—to the police, to the town, to Emile. Mrs. Okonkwo's letter to her dead daughter becomes her model: words that exist to be true, not received. The beat is the writer learning her own craft's hardest lesson.

chapters.title: Gus's Last Letter
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Gus dies; his daughter gives Rosalind a letter he asked her to write for him weeks earlier—addressed to Emile, confessing he saw Rosalind's mother that night and stayed silent to protect a neighbor's family. The beat is grief braided with revelation: silence was the town's shared currency.

chapters.title: The Fire That Didn't Happen
chapters.summary: Climax, part one. Voss, exposed by Rosalind's research as having falsified the original insurance angle to depress the lot's price, moves to demolish the site illegally before her appeal filing. Rosalind stands on the lot at night; a confrontation with Voss's crew; she reads her mother's name aloud to the town gathering. The beat is the private becoming public.

chapters.title: Testimony, Second Draft
chapters.summary: Climax, part two. At the reopened inquiry, Rosalind testifies to what she saw and what she concealed, accepting that she may implicate herself in obstruction. Emile, present, hears the truth he spent eleven years not asking for. The beat is justice outside the law: not verdict, but acknowledgment.

chapters.title: What the Court Cannot Give
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The inquiry finds the conviction unsafe but charges no one; the law's limits are plain. Emile, furious and freed in the same hour, disappears. Rosalind, facing her own possible charges, waits—and finds she can breathe anyway. The beat is the anticlimax that is actually the point.

chapters.title: The Empty Lot
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She declines Voss's final offer, keeps the lot, and plants nothing: a garden of stones and one bench, a place for the town to sit with what it did. She writes letters again—but now she teaches others to send them while the recipients live. The beat is belonging rebuilt from wreckage.

chapters.title: A Letter, Addressed and Sent
chapters.summary: Rosalind's and Emile's POVs, converging. A postcard arrives at Emile's boatyard, correctly addressed, four sentences long, asking nothing. He reads it twice, writes back three words, and mails it. Final image: two addresses, no longer burning. The beat is resolution as correspondence, not reunion.
